https://www.emsnow.com/how-the-new-gener.text: How the New Generation of Advanced Lasers Could Supercharge The Robotic Revolution September 10, 2026 Analysis , Europe , Industrial , Robotics A femtosecond laser mounted on a robotic arm could do high-value precision tasks and significantly increase productivity in fields ranging from electronics manufacturing to semiconductors and medicine. According to LITILIT, the current limiting factor for such applications is femtosecond laser size. By Nikolajus Gavrilinas, co-founder and CEO of LITILIT. (Source: LITILIT) The AI boom has accelerated interest in robotics, with the global robotics market expected to grow dramatically over the next decade. According to experts at femtosecond laser company LITILIT, recent advancements in robotics make new industrial robotic systems strong and precise enough to trade their screwdrivers and grippers for precision tools like advanced lasers. During the first half of this year, investments in robotics increased to $47.4 billion, up 80% compared to the same period last year, according to Crunchbase calculations. Industry analysts forecast that the robotics market could grow by around 25 times by 2035 on average, while a Barclays report estimates that the humanoid robotics market could grow from today’s 2-3 billion USD to 200 billion USD in the most optimistic scenario. Humanoid robots are expected to account for a significant part of that expansion, easing labor shortages, automating repetitive workflows and taking over physically demanding or hazardous work across manufacturing, logistics, agriculture, and healthcare, the report claims. According to Nikolajus Gavrilinas, co-founder and CEO of laser manufacturing company LITILIT , the advancements in robotics also present a great opportunity for higher-value manufacturing. As industrial robots become more powerful and precise, they can be equipped with more advanced tools such as femtosecond lasers. “Most industrial robots today are used with tools for gripping, screwdriving, bolting, drilling, packing, or similar tasks. Once you equip the same machine with an advanced laser, it can move into a different category of work: precision manufacturing. That means processing materials with much higher accuracy and creating more value from the same automated platform,” Gavrilinas says. Femtosecond lasers use extremely short pulses that can process materials without damaging nearby structures. This makes them useful in high-precision applications where even small amounts of heat can affect the material being processed. Mounted on a robotic system, such a laser could perform tasks such as drilling through-glass vias in semiconductor interposers, cutting curved cover glass for foldable phones, and marking durable traceability codes onto electric vehicle batteries, according to Gavrilinas. However, the main obstacle to such applications is laser size. Many femtosecond lasers are too large and complex to be mounted directly on a moving robotic system. Gavrilinas says reducing size was a deliberate design goal for LITILIT, and its units run 1.5 to 2 times smaller than a typical femtosecond laser. “Most femtosecond lasers historically came from scientific systems. They can deliver strong performance, but they are often large, complex, and require periodic maintenance. Our lasers use a modular design, a high level of automation and reduced component complexity, making them compact enough for robotic integration and practical enough for industrial use,” he explains. The same architecture also lets LITILIT manufacture advanced lasers at scale. LITILIT is currently developing a femtosecond laser factory in Vilnius and plans to start laser production this October. Over the next few years, the company plans to manufacture up to 3,000 lasers per year, on track to become one of the highest-capacity femtosecond laser factories in the world. LITILIT builds lasers based on a few patented inventions ( patent 1 , patent 2 ), made by LITILIT co-founders Kęstutis Regelskis, Nerijus Rusteika, and Gavrilinas, in close collaboration with the Center for Physical Sciences and Technology (FTMC) in Vilnius. Photograph: Mouneb Taim/Anadolu/Getty Images Opinion Gaza How Gaza changed Europe, exposing cracks that grow bigger by the week Shada Islam Solidarity with Palestine’s suffering is punished but MEPs allow a witch-hunt of European Muslims Thu 15 Oct 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 00.01 EDT Share F or three painful years, Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza, in retaliation for the Hamas terror attacks on 7 October 2023, has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians , wounded thousands more and reduced most of the territory to rubble. It has changed views of Israel across the world , increased support for Palestine and raised questions about US power. Europe’s failure to hold Israel’s government to account has cost it global credibility and influence. But I fear something even more consequential than that: Gaza is changing Europe itself. European governments did nothing to try to stop the genocide; there have been no collective sanctions , no trade restrictions or ending of arms sales to Israel. The EU sanctions Russia over its war in Ukraine but retains almost-business-as-usual ties with Israel, a blatant double standard. Gaza has exposed how Europe’s supposedly universal commitment to human rights is now conditional on whose suffering is recognised , whose resistance is considered legitimate and whose demands for justice are considered worthy of attention. EU policymakers are selective even in the groups of women they choose to celebrate as heroic in struggles against occupation and the children whose right to life they defend. After these three years I am convinced that the question of Palestine has become a stress test for European democracy itself. Democratic societies can only thrive when there is space for dissent, including dissent that is uncomfortable, disruptive and politically inconvenient. Yet today, across Europe, governments – which speak up against undemocratic conduct abroad – are now unapologetic in imposing restrictions on free expression and peaceful protest at home. Police violence at pro-Palestinian demonstrations has become the norm, and those whose only crime is to speak up publicly for Palestinian rights are increasingly criminalised or made the target of suspicion. When this happens repeatedly it undermines public trust in the legitimacy of democratic governments and institutions. As Rabin Baldewsingh, the Netherlands’ national coordinator against discrimination and racism tells me: “Governments and public institutions have a responsibility not to reinforce polarisation when society is deeply divided.” Sadly, the opposite appears to be happening. Many societal fractures existed before Gaza, but they have received new oxygen and traction over the past three years. The EU’s Fundamental Rights Agency has long warned of both anti-Muslim racism and antisemitism . What has become increasingly troubling over the past three years is the political framing under which antisemitism in connection with Gaza is rightly treated as a threat to democracy, while Islamophobia is viewed through a security and anti-terrorism lens. This can’t all be blamed on the far right, either. True, some extremist groups hide their age-old prejudices behind accusations that it is Muslims and refugees who have “imported” antisemitism into Europe. But the European People’s party (EPP) – the EU’s largest political “family” for pro-European centre-right and conservative politicians, including Ursula von der Leyen and Magnus Brunner, the EU’s most senior official for migration – is also giving old and debunked Islamophobic tropes a new and dangerous lease of life. The party backed a resolution in June condemning the “interference of political Islam” in European democratic processes. If “political Islam” was interfering in European democracy, the resolution may have some validity. But there is no evidence for the claim, and certainly none advanced in this document, which merely echoes French conspiracy theories about “ Islamist entryism ” and calls for a crackdown on alleged members of Muslim Brotherhood networks. It claims to make a distinction between “political Islam” and the Islamic faith itself but it reads more like the start of a witch-hunt of European Muslims. An even tougher EPP resolution, backed by a majority in the European parliament on 8 October, goes a step further by casting suspicion on Muslim civil society groups’ loyalty, activity and participation in European democracy. Hiba Latreche, president of Femyso , a pan-European network of young Muslim organisations that is explicitly mentioned in the EPP’s attack, points out the double bind of such unfounded allegations. “When we are not active we are accused of communitarianism, separatism and lack of integration. When we engage and exercise active citizenship we are accused of having a hidden agenda.” Such an environment demands even stronger anti-discrimination action. Yet Europe’s most powerful pro-equality body, the European Network Against Racism (ENAR), has just lost European Commission funding. Worried that this could mean it has to cease operations by the end of the year, ENAR has launched a legal challenge against the decision at the EU’s general court. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Beyond the visible, there are many unwritten post-Gaza codes being applied inside the EU’s corridors of power that are harder to measure and challenge. Islamophobia has become “quite blatant”, EU officials tell me, with micro‑aggressions and remarks about Muslims’ supposedly “irrational and emotional” behaviour. Like von der Leyen in her recent “state of the union” speech , many now talk about Gaza as a humanitarian emergency, but not as a human-made genocide. There is agreement on the need for action against settler violence and illegal settlement in the West Bank, which is framed as the work of “extremists”, but confronting the Israeli government remains difficult. For many, it has also been a time of uncomfortable conversations, ruptured personal relationships and disillusionment. But there are also moments of intense solidarity, as across Europe pro‑Palestinian movements have extended to include trade unions, faith groups – including Jewish activists – students, celebrities and senior politicians. Every Thursday, members of the EU Staff for Peace gather for a vigil outside the commission and the EU Council. Former EU commissioners, ambassadors and senior staff continue to write to their bosses urging stronger action against Israel. So all hope is not lost. But Gaza has stripped away a great deal of self-soothing assumptions that many of us harboured about Europe . As the far right becomes more influential, too many have forgotten that democratic freedoms rarely disappear all at once. They begin to erode when some voices are silenced, some suffering is ignored and the rights of some citizens are treated as less deserving than others. VPNs are no longer just for corporate IT departments and tech-obsessed tinkerers. These days, remote workers rely on them for everyday access, and chances are your favorite creator has already tried to pitch you one during a podcast ad break. But beyond the marketing hype, do you actually need one? From hiding your activity on public Wi-Fi to shielding your data from hungry ISPs, let's cut through the noise and break down everything a VPN can—and can't—do so you can make the right call.

How a VPN Encrypts Your Connection

VPN stands for "virtual private network." Consider your home router and Wi-Fi connection as your personal private network. Whenever you browse the internet on your private network, that data is visible and traceable back to you by anyone with access to that connection. Entities that could potentially see that data include your ISP, advertisers, trackers, and malicious snoopers.

Connecting to a VPN transforms that readable data into an incomprehensible string of characters through a process called encryption. This encrypted data arrives at the VPN’s server through a secure ‘tunnel.’ This data would be unreadable to anyone who got hold of it in transit. Once your data arrives at the server, it is decrypted and sent to its original destination. After that, anyone trying to trace that information back to you will hit a dead end, as that data only goes back to the VPN server. This process severs your connection to that web traffic, and a good VPN won’t store any of its users' decrypted data. Data coming back to your device makes the same trip: from the internet, to the VPN server, through the encrypted connection, and back to your machine.

When most people talk about VPNs, they are likely referring to services aimed at consumers. However, VPNs have broader applications and have been in use for decades. Before the great VPN boom, corporations used VPNs to let workers access digital resources remotely, long before many of us started working from home.

If you are getting a VPN for personal use, you don't necessarily need another company to set it up. There are a few options to set up your own, such as OpenVPN, or you can build one with some know-how and spare PC parts or a Raspberry Pi. Doing so can be complicated if you’re not tech-savvy or used to working with PCs. You'll also need to rent or maintain that VPN server yourself, which is definitely more difficult (and more prone to security risks) than paying a VPN service to handle it. While there are some things you can do to make a self-hosted VPN more accessible, it's usually best left to tinkerers who don’t mind the upkeep and regular maintenance required to keep its coverage consistent.

How a VPN Works

The Anonymity Myth: What a VPN Can (and Can't) Hide

It is nearly impossible to be 100% anonymous online. Someone somewhere has a trace of your data as long as you’re connected to an internet service provider (ISP). That said, a VPN makes it a lot harder for anyone to track your precise movements, location, and activity.

Take your ISP, for example. It knows everything you do online, from the sites you visit to the files you download. There’s nothing private about it. You choose your provider (if you’re lucky enough to have multiple options in your region) for access to the internet, but the payment doesn’t stop there. ISPs are known to aggregate and sell user data. This isn’t some hidden practice either. While these services don’t flaunt the fact that they do this, it is often buried within the privacy policy when you sign up.

The FTC issued a report back in 2021 outlining exactly how much your ISP knows about what you do online. It’s likely even more than you’d expect. Your ISP can sell that anonymized customer data. While that data does not have your name directly attached to it, you’re still being profited off of by a provider that, more often than not, you are forced to use thanks to a lack of competition.

That’s where a VPN comes in. It can cut off that data feed and restore some of your privacy. Again, it can’t stop everything, but it can reduce that flood of data to a trickle. The ISP won’t be able to see any of your web data. It can still see how much data you use, when you use it, and whatever personal information you had to give to sign up.

Aside from the ever-looming eye of your ISP, VPNs also make it harder for advertisers to track you online. Many advertisers use data connected to your IP address to target advertisements and monitor your habits. A VPN removes that data source by making it appear as though your traffic is originating elsewhere. Unfortunately, advertisers have other tools to monitor you that a VPN can’t prevent. Cookies and trackers are on most sites you visit. When you click ‘accept’ on a cookie pop-up, you allow those sites and their advertisers to track your habits on their site and beyond. A VPN alone can't do anything about that (although many offer tools to help).
